analysis.one_liner: Quadruples the stock buyback tax to 25% for large oil and gas companies while gasoline prices are high.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in May 2026 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has seen no further action and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill raises the federal excise tax on corporate stock buybacks from 1% to 25% for oil and gas companies with over $1 billion in annual receipts. The higher rate kicks in when regular gasoline sells for at least $2.937 per gallon and stays in effect until prices fall below that level for five straight weeks. The idea is to discourage big oil companies from using windfall profits during price spikes to buy back their own stock rather than invest in production, and to raise revenue from buybacks that do happen.
analysis.who_benefits: Motorists and the general public benefit indirectly: a 25% tax makes buybacks during price spikes much more expensive, encouraging companies to direct cash toward production, dividends, or lower prices instead. The Treasury also collects revenue from any buybacks that still occur, which reduces the deficit burden on taxpayers.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the excise tax on stock buybacks by large oil and gas companies from 1% to 25%, making buybacks far more expensive when gasoline prices are high.

The higher rate applies to companies with $1 billion or more in average annual gross receipts that are primarily engaged in producing, refining, processing, transporting, or distributing oil or natural gas.
The 25% rate stays in effect until the weekly retail price of regular gasoline is below $2.937 per gallon for five consecutive weeks, automatically sunsetting when prices fall.

analysis.who_pays: Large oil and gas companies and their shareholders bear the cost: buybacks of their own stock during periods of high gasoline prices would face a 25% excise tax instead of the current 1%. Oil executives whose pay is tied to buyback-driven share price gains also lose a favored tool for boosting stock value.

drawbacks.text: The tax is triggered by the retail gasoline price, not by actual company profits, so it can apply to buybacks even in years when a company's earnings are ordinary — despite the 'windfall' name.

Economists disagree about whether buybacks reduce supply; companies can shift to dividends, which the bill does not tax, and critics argue the tax raises consumer costs little if production is unchanged.
The 25% rate is 25 times the current federal buyback tax, a steep enough penalty that it functions more as a prohibition during price spikes than a modest levy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit to the public is real but indirect: it raises revenue and changes incentives at oil companies, but it does not directly lower gasoline prices, and the price trigger means the tax can bite even without proven excess profits. The cost falls squarely on a concentrated industry during exactly the periods when its prices — and likely its profits — are highest, which is the point. The main design weakness is using the gas pump price as a proxy for windfall profits.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late May 2026 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which has not acted on it and no vote has been scheduled.

narrative.text: Senator Wyden introduced the bill on May 20, 2026, with 16 Democratic cosponsors including the Senate party leader.
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance, and no further action has been taken since.
No Republicans have cosponsored the bill, and Republicans hold 55 of 100 Senate seats, including the Finance Committee majority.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large oil and gas companies and their shareholders are better off so far: the bill sits untouched in committee, leaving buybacks at their current 1% tax rate.

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise the buyback excise tax to 25% for large oil and gas companies.

for.name: 16 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors, including the Senate party leader

sides.party_line_note: All 16 cosponsors are Democrats and no Republicans have signed on; with Republicans holding 55 Senate seats, the bill has faced no votes yet, so opposition has taken the form of inaction rather than recorded votes.

industries.note: A 25% tax on buybacks during high gasoline prices directly reduces a tool these companies use to return cash to shareholders and lift stock prices. The industry has historically argued buybacks do not reduce investment in production; the bill's premise is that during price spikes, buybacks come at the public's expense.

industries.industry: Oil company shareholders, including pension funds
industries.note: Shareholders of covered companies would receive less buyback-driven support for share prices, though the tax could push companies toward dividends, which are not treated differently here. Many shareholders are ordinary investors through retirement funds.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the Senate Finance Committee, where Republicans hold the majority and no markups or votes are scheduled. A new excise tax increase on a major industry has little path to floor time under divided Senate control; the most likely outcome is that it stays in committee until the Congress ends. Its main near-term value may be as a messaging vehicle if gasoline prices spike.
